name: Red light therapy for scalp

lead: Red light therapy uses low-power lasers or LEDs in caps, combs, helmets or panels over thinning areas, aiming to slow hair loss and thicken hair. It is a non-drug, at-home add-on to other treatments.

Proponents say the light stimulates cell function and healing in follicles. Reviews range from little evidence (2012) to tentative benefit (2014, 2015, 2017), with a 2017 review reporting improvement in 10 of 11 trials and a 2019 meta-analysis favouring lasers over LEDs; some reviews note high risk of bias and call for longer trials.

paras: People wear a cap or helmet or pass a comb or panel over the scalp for short sessions several times a week, usually alongside minoxidil or finasteride, and use it over months.

Reported effects are mild pain or skin irritation, and long-term effects are unknown. Eye protection is suggested for some devices, response may vary by skin type, and dermatologist advice is suggested. Some marketers have faced FDA action over unsupported claims.

web.title: Photobiomodulation for the management of alopecia
Lasers in the management of alopecia

angle.text: Users wear light caps or use combs and panels on thinning areas, aiming to stimulate follicles for denser hair and slower thinning. It is a non-drug at-home add-on, and several reviews report tentative benefit while calling for better long-term trials.

lead: Red light therapy for the scalp applies low-power red or near-infrared light, from a laser or LED cap, helmet, comb or panel, to the head. People use it to thicken thinning hair and slow pattern hair loss so the hairline and crown look fuller. It belongs to low-level laser therapy, also called photobiomodulation, which uses light roughly in the 600 to 950 nanometer range.[1][2]

The generally proposed mechanism is that light is absorbed by cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondria, which may raise cellular energy production; for androgenetic alopecia, reviewers suggest this could activate follicle stem cells and move follicles toward the growth phase.[1][3] Devices such as the HairMax LaserComb have received FDA clearance after manufacturer-sponsored, sham-controlled trials.[2]

Review conclusions have shifted over time: a 2012 review found little support, 2014 and 2015 reviews reported tentative benefit or mixed results, and a 2017 review found that 10 of 11 trials showed improvement in androgenetic alopecia.[1] In looksmaxxing and hair-loss communities it is discussed as a non-drug add-on alongside minoxidil and finasteride.
infobox: 10 to 25 minutes per session, 3 times weekly to daily, for 16 to 26 weeks[3][2]
Several devices FDA-cleared for hair growth[1][2]
Dry skin, itching, irritation, mild headache[3][2]

paras: Scalp light therapy is sold as hats and helmets, handheld combs or brushes, headbands and stationary hoods, and some units are panels or masks.[3] Most devices use low-power red laser diodes of about 5 milliwatts, typically at 630 to 660 nm, and some add LEDs.[3] Laser combs are described as better at parting hair so that light reaches the scalp.[3]

Reviewers describe use as a scheduled routine that continues for months. Hamblin's 2019 review notes that home devices are usually used once a day, sometimes every second day, with sessions of roughly 10 to 20 minutes, and that benefit requires consistent use over months, which may lead some users to stop early.[3] Wikipedia reports that a 2019 comparative meta-analysis found device type (hat, comb or helmet) and treatment duration did not change effectiveness, and that another 2019 analysis favored lasers over LEDs.[1]

The leading hypothesis is that light stimulates cytochrome c oxidase in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, possibly by releasing inhibitory nitric oxide, increasing respiration and ATP production.[1][3] For androgenetic alopecia, Hamblin proposes that light energises bulge stem cells, which normally rely on low-oxygen, glycolytic metabolism, and that a brief rise in reactive oxygen species may help push them toward differentiation and the growth (anagen) phase.[3]

The 2024 review in Lasers in Medical Science lists further proposed effects: moving telogen follicles back into anagen, prolonging anagen, improving microcirculation, and anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions. It states that there is no clear consensus on the mechanism.[2] For alopecia areata Hamblin suggests a shift of macrophages from a pro-inflammatory to a repair-oriented state.[3] Wikipedia notes that doses below the effective range appear to do nothing.[1]

Endre Mester (1903 to 1984), a Hungarian physician who began laser research in 1965, observed while applying low-intensity laser light to shaved mice that hair regrew faster on treated animals; he published the work in 1967.[4] The observation is widely cited as a starting point for low-level laser therapy, and Mester began treating patients with non-healing skin ulcers in 1971 and founded a laser research center at Semmelweis University in 1974.[4]

The first commercial hair devices followed decades later. A 2009 sham-controlled trial of the HairMax LaserComb, sponsored by its maker Lexington International, was followed by FDA clearance of the device.[2] Marketing of unvalidated light devices has also drawn regulatory action: in 2014 the FDA sued QLaser PMA for promoting its devices for more than 200 diseases, a permanent injunction followed in 2015, and in 2018 its owner Robert Lytle pleaded guilty to fraud conspiracy and was sentenced to 12 years in prison.[1]

Different wavelengths are discussed for different conditions. A 2022 meta-analysis summarised by Wikipedia suggested ultraviolet and infrared light work better for alopecia areata, while red and infrared light work better for androgenetic alopecia.[1] Barikbin and colleagues compared a 655 nm laser cap with a combined 655 and 808 nm scanner in 90 people, and both improved hair counts, with the combined wavelengths slightly better.[3]

Light is often used alongside topical minoxidil. Esmat and colleagues' trial in women is the one study cited by Hamblin that tested the pairing directly, and it found benefit appearing earlier, by two months, with the combination than with either treatment alone.[3] Hamblin also lists combination with hair transplantation or platelet-rich plasma as suggested uses that have not been tested in published trials.[3]

Hamblin writes that men and women with androgenetic alopecia both respond, that treatment is best started when thinning first appears, and that follicles lost in fully bald scalp are unlikely to recover.[3] He notes that darker skin (Fitzpatrick types IV to VI) may need longer exposure than lighter skin, a point he says has not been tested in a trial, and that thick dark hair can block light but this may matter less where hair is already thinning.[3] Wikipedia reports that responses may vary by skin type, race and ethnicity and suggests consulting a dermatologist; in the US it recommends devices cleared by the FDA for dermatologic use.[1]

Leavitt and colleagues' double-blind, sham-controlled trial of 110 men with androgenetic alopecia used a 655 nm comb for 15 minutes three times a week for 26 weeks. Hamblin reports a hair density gain of about 17 hairs per square centimeter in the active group against a loss of about 9 in the sham group.[3][2] The trial was sponsored by the device maker.[2]

Jimenez and colleagues' multicenter trial of 141 women and 128 men used the comb three times weekly for 26 weeks and found a larger increase in terminal hairs than sham, regardless of age or sex, with more active users reporting improved thickness and fullness.[2] Kim and colleagues' 24-week trial of 40 people used a helmet-type device with 630, 650 and 660 nm light; the active group gained about 17 hairs per square centimeter against a loss of about 2 in the sham group, and hair thickness also increased.[3][2] Lanzafame and colleagues studied 44 men and 47 women with a 655 nm helmet used every second day for 16 weeks, reporting hair count rises of 62.5 percent versus 37 percent for sham in men and 48 percent versus 11 percent in women.[3]

In Esmat and colleagues' four-month trial of 45 women with female pattern hair loss, topical 5% minoxidil, light therapy and the combination all increased hair counts on ultrasound biomicroscopy in the light and combination groups, but only the combination improved significantly on the Ludwig classification, and the combination group reported higher satisfaction.[3][2] Yamazaki and colleagues treated 15 people with patchy alopecia areata and reported regrowth in 46.7 percent of treated areas, about 1.6 months earlier than untreated areas.[3] Hamblin found no published clinical trial for chemotherapy-induced alopecia, and animal studies in mice and rats have reported regrowth with 655 nm laser in alopecia areata and chemotherapy models.[3]

Review authors note limitations. Several studies had small samples and possible bias, some were sponsored by manufacturers, and Hamblin's own conflict-of-interest statement lists advisory and consulting roles with device companies including Lexington International.[3][2] Wikipedia describes the 2012 review as finding little support, the 2014 and 2015 reviews as tentative benefit, one 2014 review as mixed with high risk of bias, and the 2017 review of clinical trials as reporting improvement in 10 of 11 androgenetic alopecia trials, and says some reviews suggest results comparable to minoxidil or finasteride but that larger randomized, long-term, double-blind trials are needed.[1]

Hamblin's review reports side effects in under 10 percent of cases, generally tolerable and transient: dryness, irritation, itching and mild headache.[3] The 2024 review reports mostly mild effects in the main trials, such as headache, mild itching, redness and dryness, with no serious adverse events, and notes that laser irradiation can generate reactive oxygen species that may contribute to redness and pigmentation.[2] Wikipedia reports some people experience mild pain or skin irritation, that long-term effects on skin and hair are unknown, and that some devices call for eye protection.[1]

lore.intro: In hair-loss and looksmaxxing discussion, scalp light caps and combs are treated as a drug-free addition to minoxidil and finasteride, and a way to hold or thicken hair without prescriptions. The claims below are as described by device makers and proponents in the published reviews.[1][3]

claims.claim: Light therapy can thicken thinning hair
Light works through mitochondria and follicle stem cells
Light therapy is about as effective as drugs
Any red light product delivers the same benefit

timeline.event: Endre Mester reports faster hair regrowth in laser-treated shaved mice.[1][4]
Mester founds the Laser Research Center at Semmelweis University.[4]
Sham-controlled trial of 110 men using a laser comb is published.[3][2]
A 24-week sham-controlled trial of 40 people with a 630 to 660 nm device is reported.[2]
Multicenter trial of 269 men and women using the comb is reported; FDA sues QLaser PMA.[1][2]
Permanent injunction against QLaser PMA over unsupported claims.[1]
Esmat and colleagues compare minoxidil, light and both in 45 women.[2]
QLaser owner pleads guilty to fraud conspiracy.[1]
Hamblin reviews photobiomodulation mechanisms and use in alopecia.[3]
